doc.title: Tom Albert and Milton "Mooney" Martin Interview, 1964-12-21

chapter: Trombonists, old string bands and dance steps
title: Tom gives Johnny Lindsey a trombone reading test
summary: Tom tells how Johnny Lindsey, a theatre-show bassist, came to his house at 512 Dolphin Street for lessons. Tom tried him on a piece in four flats with a short-shank and long-shank trombone, then told him he could go. Russell says Lindsey died around 1948.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Well, I want to tell you something about this boy playing trombone. Lindsay boy. Oh, yeah.
Johnny. I heard him on bass. I never heard him on trombone.

You heard him on bass? Yeah, in Chicago. He used to play with, uh, what he used to play with? A robot show. Well, he used to play at a robot show. Well, he used to play at a robot show. I'm trying more. So, he was playing at the palace. He was playing at the palace and, uh, so he, he was a good reader. But he wasn't sure. You understand? Yeah. Yeah. So, he asked me, he said, tell him I want to take a couple of lessons. I live at 512 Dolphin Street. So, I say, yes, come on. But he could play and I was getting that music. I used to get two copies every month at, uh, in New York, Daniels, and going to that club. Yeah. Yeah. I believe they're in the business now. You send us two copies every, every, uh, every month.

So, I say, yes. And I live at 512 Dolphin Street. So, we came there when he, uh, had, uh, on the recess, do you understand? He came over to my house and, uh, put on some music, and the tram on for it. I had my contact, you understand? Playing with him. And, uh, but he really put it good, but he wasn't sure.
I used to, uh, I had a horse come from Little Feast. And I believe it was in about, it was about, uh, three or four flats from him. Yeah. And, uh, uh, had trouble with it.

And, uh, and I played it two, three times. That's the time we used to pull out, I had two shanks then. Oh, yeah. You see? Yeah. I remember how they did that. We'd take the short shank out and put the long shank in. Well, I was in, uh, in G, you know, and put him in F, you know, we played tram on. And, uh, so, I said last night I'd give him two lessons. And I, you know, he said, why the music is good? I used to, like, you know. And I, in that horse, do, I said, do, I'll try anymore. Well, he knew all that. And I played that once, and we had him in four flats, I believe. And I played it, I said, he reads good. When I was out there, then he was there too.

And, uh, well, I said, he's all right. And, uh, so I played it, I said, come on, let's play this again. I wasn't sure. And I played it again, and I went, one, two, three. The way he played it, he played it. I said, you can go. And I never seen him anymore.
Yeah, he died about, um, oh, around 1948 or so, along in there. Yeah. But I never seen him anymore. After I said, you can go.
Well, he was playing the rover show then. But he wasn't sure. Yeah. The division, you understand. He could play with the division.
Yeah. He was, his time and the division and all that.
